#1977. RECAP: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Man City - Premier League: Enzo Maresca's men suffer third defeat in a row, as Liam Delap stars to lift his side out of drop zone - at Man United's expense

RDaily Mail Sport's live coverage of Nottingham Forest vs Man City.

Oliver Glasner channelled his inner Jose Mourinho when Delap scored Forest's third goal, sprinting down the touchline to celebrate with his players.

In such a precarious job, this victory will mean a lot to him. There's never any guarantee of owner Evangelos Marinakis' patience.

For the first time since 2024, Manchester City have lost three consecutive games in the top fliight.

They're also just the second team in top-flight history to win their first seven games then lose the next three. The previous side to do that were Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05.

I suspect they'll beat Fulham after the international break, but you never know!

Manchester United end a day in the bottom three of the to -flight after having played at least nine games for the first time since November 1986.

Ouch. Thanks to Opta for the stat. They'll be looking to make amends against Aston Villa tomorrow but I don't back them.

Donnarumma had another poor game today, looking flappy. I'm not sure there was much he could have done about the goals, which were all worthy strikes, but conceding three goals won't help a man who has come under increasing scrutiny in recent weeks.

Here's why Maresca stood by him. Do you think it's time for a change?

Why Maresca is sticking with Donnarumma despite Leipzig horror show

JACK GAUGHAN: These are tough times for Donnarumma, a calamitous night in the Champions League adding to the feeling that the past few weeks have not reflected kindly on him.

Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol looked lost today. Enzo Maresca hooked the at half-time after each was at fault for one of the goals. Gvardiol was asleep, giving away the ball for the first, and Guehi just retreated as Delap ran towards goal for the second.

Worrying. Guehi has looked shorn of confidence in recent weeks and this isn't the first time he's been withdrawn at the break.

Today we saw the version of Delap which we know he can be. An absolute bulldozer.

His main flaw is that he typically lacks the finishing. To demonstrate: coming into today, he had scored just two Premier League goals since the start of LAST season. Not a good look.

Well, his finishing was explosive here, as was his running and strength. He's scary when he plays like that.

Manchester United have never been in the relegation zone at this stage of a Premier League season before. Truly abysmal for them.

As for Forest, they can smile after being rewarded for their good performance. They're far from out of the woods, but they did two key things today: score at home, and get Liam Delap's confidence up. Both are critical.

Maresca straight down the tunnel and it didn’t seem as if there was a handshake between him and Oliver Glasner. Dismal night for City but the performance is in keeping with how they are playing. So susceptible on the break and when you’re making this many individual mistakes then the opponents know that they can just wait for them.

Liam Delap has been speaking to Sky Sports.

'It's been coming. We've been performing like that every week but not putting it in the net,' he said.

'We did everything right, got the three points, and are happy going into the international break.

'I just wanted to run and shoot and luckily go there and it went in the net (for first goal).

'Thankfully I put it in the net (for the second).

'We'll have to see it back (Glasner's run down the touchline). Never (seen him run like that).

'We've been deserving this for a long time. Hopefully we can build on it.'

Man City have now lost three times on the spin in the Premier League. Whatever faux title charge they were mounting is collapsing fast at this rate.

The full time whistle blows an Oliver Glasner fist pumps. A HUGE win for Nottingham Forest, one which propels them out of the relegation zone, and plunges Manchester United into it.

#1976. Celtic have opened the door to Rangers being 'No1 in Scotland again' - ex-manager

Celtic are not getting enough elite performances from their star players - and that has opened the door to Rangers.

That is according to ex-manager and experienced former Tottenham, Aston Villa and Everton scout, Bryan King, speaking exclusively to Football Insider.

The Hoops have struggled for consistency this season so far, winning just five of their last 12 games across all competitions.

Martin O'Neill had not expected to remain in charge of Celtic when he returned last season, and he has now faced mounting pressure after taking the job permanently once more.

But the problems at Celtic Park are considered to come from the top, with largest individual shareholder Dermot Desmond among several targets of discontent among the fanbase.

The Scottish champions currently sit top of the Premiership, with Rangers to have the chance to go within a point when they play their game in hand.

🗞️ Manager delighted to get important win over Kilmarnock🔗 - https://t.co/bkBwLvzExv #CELKIL | #CelticFC🍀 pic.twitter.com/MXMYM8AUpY

Kasper Hogh is one example of a player struggling to adapt to life since making the switch to Celtic.

The striker was a force with Bodo/Glimt in Norway, but has failed to score a single goal since netting a hat-trick on just his second appearance for the club in August.

"Just have a look at what's happened to Celtic as a team. They've been rather inconsistent," King told Football Insider when asked about Hogh.

"They've performed badly in Europe. There seems to be problems every week within the unit, and it's all about confidence.

"The centre forward's got to be scoring goals, but he can only score goals if the service is right. And now he's getting into a situation where Celtic haven't exactly been setting the Scottish league alight.

"They've been losing games which you wouldn't expect them to lose, which has allowed Rangers to start looking as though they could be the number one team in Scotland again.

"There are things not right within that football club as we speak, Celtic."

O'Neill's return last season ultimately saved Celtic from an abysmal season.

Brendan Rodgers had resigned in October and his eventual replacement, Wilfried Nancy, lasted just over a month before he was sacked.

O'Neill returned again and led his team to the Scottish Premiership and cup double - which many thought would be his last feat in charge of the Hoops.

But in extending his contract, Celtic have kicked the can down the road for next summer, when they will inevitably have to make a decision.

Then, without O'Neill to hold them back, the true extent of the problems at Parkhead may well emerge.

Two goals from Domeiro Bobb-Semple, one in each half, put the Bees 2-0 up and a late debut goal for Connor Wickham wasn’t enough for the home side.

Reds fans might have hoped this compeition – which brought a big win over Bromley last month – could again lift some of the gloom surrounding the club during a poor first half of the season.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

But just two days after their embarrassing FA Cup exit at Wimborne Town, it was another setback for interim boss Kevin Blackwell and his players.

Blackwell made 10 changes from that performance at the weekend against Wimborne. Only Vito Mannone kept his place, and new signing Ayman Benarous started the game, with the other new face Wickham starting on the bench.

In a fairly even first half, both sides played some good flowing football. However, it was the Bees who took the lead on 27 minutes. It was soon 2-0 when yet another Mrisho error allowed Gustavo Gomez the space to pick out Bobb-Semple to fire home for his second goal of the night. The game settled down a little after that flurry of action.

Rose in the Brentford goal had to make a couple of saves, one from an Aderoju header, and he got a hand to a Klaudio Krasniqi shot, which was possibly going over anyway. Riley Owen fired a shot straight at Mannone midway through the second half.

Crawley’s other new signing, Wickham, managed to open his account for the Reds with a late penalty after Malcolm Ebowei was fouled in the box, to make it 2-1, but it wasn’t enough to put Crawley through.

Crawley now have 10 days off – their planned league game with Rotherham this weekend is postponed due to international call ups. The Reds next game is Fleetwood Town at home on November 21.

#1973. Ex-Tottenham scout drops explosive Mykhailo Mudryk verdict

Mykhailo Mudryk and Alejandro Garnacho's situations at Tottenham Hotspur and Aston Villa are comparable.

That is the opinion of former senior Villa and Tottenham scout, Bryan King, speaking exclusively to Football Insider.

Mudryk, who arrived on loan from Chelsea on transfer deadline day, has been unavailable with an ankle injury for over two months after making his debut.

The winger was banned from featuring for nearly two years after he tested positive for a banned substance with the FA finally clearing him to play in July.

Tottenham have a £75million option to buy Mudryk but have yet to see him feature for more than 16 minutes, with his return possibly to come after the international break.

Garnacho, while not injured, has struggled just as much for minutes since signing for Villa on loan from Chelsea with an obligation to buy next summer.

Still not a single update about Mykhailo Mudryk who was supposed to return from his ankle injury after the international break…🤷‍♂️I know he’s only on loan (with an option to buy for £75M 🤣), but surely this has to go down as one of the worst #THFC  signings of all time? pic.twitter.com/4WL9rOL7pY

Should Garnacho reach a certain amount of appearances for Villa this season, he will be signed permanently.

But the Argentina international has made only seven so far this season, and is seriously struggling to make any more.

Sunday's clash at Manchester United saw him left out of the squad again - the third time in the last four Premier League matches.

"I've got a nice answer for that. No. I couldn't see him making an impact before it, let alone after it," King told Football Insider when asked about Mudryk's chances of returning in form.

"I think the whole thing around Mudryk is that he came to Chelsea for an inflated fee, which I could never believe that anybody would pay that kind of money for him.

"He's been banned more through offences outside of football than he is from actually getting involved in football.

"I think we've got a situation here at Tottenham with Mudryk, which is very similar to Aston Villa's with Garnacho.

"You've got two players who are, supposedly, very talented, got a bit of pace, but look how many games Mudryk has played in the last two years.

"And Tottenham take him on? Who do they think is running the club? Aladdin? 'Come on, Mudryk, rub the lamp.'

"I'm afraid he does nothing for me, and if ever there's not a Tottenham player, he's one."

Come next summer, both Mudryk and Garnacho could well be making their returns to Stamford Bridge.

It seems incredibly unlikely that the former will be signed permanently by Tottenham, especially not for £75m.

And for Garnacho, the case of Harvey Elliott will likely have him fearing the worst already.

The Liverpool man went on loan to Villa with an obligation to buy in the summer of 2025, only for Unai Emery to decide that he did not want him and hand him only nine appearances all season.

#1970. “I don’t know why…” – John Aldridge fears Liverpool’s stance on one player could ‘backfire’

John Aldridge has questioned why Liverpool weren’t more assertive in pulling Dominik Szoboszlai out of national team duty when he’s currently nursing a minor injury.

The midfielder sprained his ankle in the 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace on Sunday, with Andoni Iraola uncertain after the game as to whether or not the 26-year-old would join up with his country during this international window.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Hungarian FA said that a decision on the player’s participation against Georgia and Northern Ireland over the next week will be deferred until the ‘last minute’ as his fitness continues to be assessed.

In his latest column for the Liverpool Echo, Aldridge voiced his belief that Liverpool should’ve done more to prevent Szoboszlai from playing for Hungary in the coming days when he’s clearly not fully fit.

The former Reds striker wrote: ‘I know Virgil van Dijk has pulled out of the Netherlands squad because of a little niggle, but Dominik Szoboszlai has stayed with Hungary despite injuring his knee against Palace.

‘Any other club would pull them out of international duty. Manchester United, Arsenal, Man City – they’d all pull them. We’ve seen it before. Any doubt and that’s it, decision made, you’re not playing. I don’t understand why we don’t throw our weight around like that.

‘I understand players want to play for their country. I was the same with Ireland. I would answer call-ups even when I was injured. I get what it means and how much it means to players, but any other club would just pull them. That’s not happened here, I don’t know why. Hopefully that just means it’s not that serious.

‘It still sounds like they’re taking a risk. If he stays with Hungary and plays, we’ve just got to hope the decision doesn’t backfire and come back to hurt Liverpool.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As Szoboszlai is contracted to Liverpool, the Merseyside club could’ve blocked him from representing his country during this international window because of his knee injury.

However, it’d appear to be a case of the player wanting to at least link up with the Hungary camp and try to prove his fitness, and Anfield chiefs green-lighting that action out of respect for the 26-year-old and not wanting to antagonise him by forbidding him to travel.

The grey area over the midfielder potentially being fit enough to play but not certain of doing so has presented a tricky dilemma, as much as Iraola would no doubt have preferred for our number 8 to swerve national team duty and prioritise his club instead.

With Hungary not playing until Saturday, that does give Szoboszlai a bit of time to recover from the knee issue he incurred at Selhurst Park, and we’d like to think that Marco Rossi wouldn’t risk fielding him against Georgia unless he’s definitely OK to feature.

While a swift return to action for the 26-year-old would obviously be a good thing, we just hope it doesn’t come at the expense of his involvement for Liverpool in the coming weeks, especially with a hectic run of 11 matches in 40 days before the end of December.

Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler will hope for good news from the treatment room during and after the international break.

Brighton still have six players unavailable but the the likes of Yankuba Minteh, Georginio, Mats Wieffer and Ferdi Kadioglu are now fit once again having spent spells on the sidelines.

Albion resume top flight action on November 22 at Hull City and will hope to welcome a number of players back to the first team picture.

Kaoru Mitoma: The Japan international is yet to feature this season due to a serious hamstring injury sustained at the back end of last season.

Hurzeler hopes to have Mitoma available for the clash at Hull but admits the 29-year-old winger may need a bit longer: “There's big belief and big hope that this will be the case,” said Hurzeler to Sussex World.

“But it might be that we need one or two weeks longer. So, I can't say this is the date or this is the game where he will be back. I think after a long injury you have to be patient with player and some players return quicker, some players need more time,

“We know that if he's back on his highest level, he will be very important for us.”

Stefanos Tzimas: The Greek striker is back in full training after his ACL injury and could be available to face Hull. “Yes, he's a little further than Kaoru,” said Hurzeler to Sussex World. “He seems to be quite on a really good level.

“He was training when we were away, and therefore I see him back on the pitch with the team after the international break.”

Pascal Struijk: The £18m arrival has struggled a bit with a thigh issue and the centre back has not featured since he was dismissed in the win at Sunderland. “With Pascal we have to go day by day.” said Hurzeler.

The international break will hopefully provide enough time for Struijk to recover but Brighton do have options at centre back with Lewis Dunk, Michael Svoboda, Luka Vuskovic and Olivier Boscagli all available.

Femi Azeez: The deadline day arrival from Millwall was “getting closer” ahead of the match against Brentford and should be available for selection at Hull City.

The Nigerian winger has gone through a fitness “adaption process” as he meets the demands of Hurzeler’s Brighton. Azeez will compete with the likes of Minteh, Diego Gomez and Zadok Yohanna for minutes on the right wing.

Zadok Yohanna: The £22m summer arrival is back training with the first team as the winger - similar to Azeez - gets up to speed with Brighton’s training methods.

The youngster should be available to face Hull City and expect him to get some minutes in the upcoming Uefa Conference League matches.

Evan Ferguson: The Ireland international striker is still recovering from ankle surgery and is yet to feature this season. Hurzeler refused to place a timeline on the striker’s potential return date and stressed the need for patience.

“We have to wait some more weeks,” said Hurzeler last month.

#1963. Scott McTominay 'had shock on heart' before Scotland World Cup game as ex-Man Utd star opens up on summer

Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay has revealed that he needed to have his heart “shocked” two days before the nation’s World Cup opener against Haiti.

McTominay explained that he was taken to hospital 48 hours before the match on June 14 and was “put to sleep”. At the time, his absence from training was put down to a sickness bug, but the 29-year-old has spoken for the first time on what he went through during the summer.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

McTominay played the full 90 minutes in the 1-0 win over the Haitians and started the next two games against Morocco and Brazil, which Scotland lost to exit the tournament at the group stage.

McTominay then went on holiday before returning to his club side Napoli, who announced on September 1 that the former Man Utd player was to have a procedure to correct a "mild benign arrhythmia". He missed the last international window under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli, but is now back in the camp for matches against North Macedonia and Switzerland in the coming days.

“I’m good,” said McTominay in his broadcast press conference on Tuesday. “I’m feeling much, much better than I was. I feel like it was something that needed to be done. In your career you have moments like that where things like that can take you by surprise. It looks a lot worse in the media for family and friends - they see news relating to a heart issue - but it’s a relatively straightforward procedure that went really well. I’m really happy to be back and playing football again. That’s the most important thing.

“I feel like it was explained to me really, really well by the doctors at Napoli and my cardiologist in Manchester alongside the doctor in Scotland when we were away at the World Cup. He explained that if this was the case, this is how it would look. Credit to all the staff members, they made me so relaxed about the situation.”

Explaining how the World Cup unfolded, McTominay continued: “The World Cup, it was difficult for me, to be honest. I had to go and get the shock on my heart. That was two days before the Haiti game. You prepare so well, I was in such good condition and something like that happens. You’re thinking ‘how has this happened to me’. But then you have to get on with it. That’s the cards you are dealt in football. Sometimes things don’t go your way and you have to continue to do your best. It’s nowhere near an excuse but it’s something you have to look back on and say ‘well, it’s part of the process.’

“Obviously the way the World Cup went, there were at least two, three weeks of me sitting there disappointed, not quite there mentally. I needed time to settle down and have a break.

“I was 100 per cent [fitness wise], but whenever you are sat in a hospital bed two days before the World Cup, about to get put to sleep, it’s not ideal, is it? So whenever things like that happen ... it is what it is, there’s nothing you can do about it. After the World Cup, I reflected on it and I was extremely disappointed. Probably the most disappointed I’ve ever been in my career.

“After the World Cup, my summer holidays weren’t heavily centred around thinking about the World Cup, but it plays a part. Whenever you are disappointed or angry about something, you go away on your holidays and it’s just not the same. You are sat there thinking ‘we could have done more’ but that three-week break I had with my operation done me the world of good.

“I’m always one to be glass half-full but after the World Cup I was like ‘this is a tough one to take’. But you have to refresh and you have to come out stronger at the other side.”

#1961. Abdsami lashes home the only goal as Hassocks leave Lingfield with a sixth consecutive win

Not many who watched Hassocks thrash Lingfield 5-1 on the opening day of the campaign would have predicted the return match at Church Road would take place with the Robins sitting fourth and the hosts fifth in the Southern Combination Premier Division.

Lingfield have improved markedly over the past three months to put themselves firmly in the playoff picture - making this 1-0 victory for Hassocks one of the Robins' most impressive results of the season.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

"A brilliant win," was how James Westlake described it afterwards. "This is a really hard place to come and play football. Not many teams will come here this season and not only win the game but also keep a clean sheet like we have done today."

The shutout was particularly impressive given Lingfield came into the fixture as the second-highest scorers in the league so far this season after Eastbourne United.

Ed Cooper made one outstanding double save late in the first half but Hassocks kept the home side relatively quiet other than that. It was a formidable performance defensively from the Robins.

A scrappy first half was lacking in quality on a playing surface which is more 1G than 3G. Omar Abdsami looked the most likely player to break the deadlock for Hassocks in the opening 45 minutes.

He had an early shot deflected over the bar and then drilled a low effort into the diving arms of Mac Chisholm after tall striker Jamie Wilkes badgered to win possession from a half-cleared Lewis Finney free kick.

Dan Turner struck a rasping volley just wide in-between those two Abdsami chances. Lingfield had their first real sight of goal when Gabriel Odunaike managed to get in one-on-one but could only fire a long way over the bar.

Next came that brilliant intervention from Cooper. Lingfield's 14-goal top scorer Kwesi Ntim tricked his way in from the left flank to draw a full stretch save on the angle out of Cooper.

The rebound fell kindly for Callum Corbin, who looked to have picked out the top corner with a powerful shot until Cooper somehow recovered and appeared from nowhere to push away the follow up.

At the start of the second half, the weather became almost as gloomy as the surroundings. Over to Adsami to brighten things up with a spectacular goal out of nothing on 53 minutes.

Blake pushed forward from right back and delivered a cross which was cleared only as far as Abdsami on the edge of the box.

Abdsami was surrounded by red and yellow striped shirts but took a touch, managed to wiggle into space and picked out the far corner with a sweeping shot giving Chisholm no chance.

A pretty special way for Abdsami to move onto double figures in his first full season of senior football.

Lingfield enjoyed a good spell after that in which they had plenty of the ball but could find no way through. Turner produced a fine piece of defending to clear away a cross which otherwise might have left Ntim with a tap in at the back post.

Otherwise, the Lingers' settled for wayward shooting from distance which posed more danger to home fans in the stand behind the goal than Cooper.

Having weathered the mini storm, it was Hassocks who finished the stronger. Lingfield committed more players forward in the closing stages and that left gaps for the Robins to exploit on the counter.

A tight offside call prevented Big Alex Fair from doubling the lead. Good hold up play from Liam Benson saw him slip Fair in for a clinical finish past Chisholm ruled out by the flag. The fact Fair took the decision with unusually good grace suggests the assistant made the correct call.

Fair then sent a header from a Finney corner towards the top corner. The Lingfield player on the near post did a remarkable job in heading it off the line to ensure his side remained in the tie.

Hassocks managed to get the ball back into the box where Benson was denied by a block and substitute Luke Brodie shot just wide from the rebound.

The Robins kept pushing and managed to rack up a couple more corners. Another taken by Finney was headed on target by Turner.

This time Chisholm pulled off a superb save to claw it out. Brodie retrieved possession and fed Fair to go around two defenders inside the area, only for a third to block his eventual shot.

Not that Hassocks needed a second goal. The full time whistle blew shortly after, followed by some strange scenes as the teams trooped off when one of the Lingfield coaching staff was accused of grabbing Turner's hand and biting it.

It was an unusual ending for a game which featured only one yellow card and showed little edge to it. Turner typically took it all in his stride as the Robins headed home chewing on a sixth consecutive win in all competitions.

Hassocks: Ed Cooper; Harvey Blake, Dan Turner, Liam Hendy, Joe Bull; Jamie Wilkes, Lewis Finney; Alex Fair, Omar Abdsami, Joe Turner; Liam Benson.

Subs: Darren Budd, Luke Brodie, Ruari Farrell (used), Lewis Croal, Charlie Bonwick-Adams (unused).

'Peak FA Cup', was the verdict from TV viewers watching (or trying to watch) the clash between Notts County and Altrincham as thick fog obscured the action.

Those tuning in on TNT Sports were baffled by what was actually happening in the game when the mist descended at Moss Lane.

Commentators saw the funny side, with Adam Summerton chuckling, saying: 'Your guess is as good as mine at the minute,' when asked by his partner what was going on.

Even though the conditions appeared to simply be deep fog, one local claimed it was smoke from local firework parties causing the white-out.

They wrote: 'It is smoke from the bonfire night fireworks and bonfires. I live round the corner, it is literally just smoke. All you can smell in the air is smoke.'

The fog is closing in at Moss Lane! 🌫️Conditions are getting tricky for Altrincham and Notts County 👀📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/gTM9e3KA2w

Fog descended on the FA Cup clash between Altrincham and Notts County and TV viewers could hardly tell what was going on

They'd had to fight back from 2-1 down in normal time after Lucas Weaver and then Lewis Banks put Altrincham in front.

#1959. Scott McTominay given police escort as drama 36 hours before Scotland World Cup clash laid bare

Scott McTominay has revealed he had to have a police escort to a hospital in Boston to have his heart ‘shocked’ 36 hours before Scotland’s opening World Cup game against Haiti.

At the time, his absence from training and travel arrangements to Boston – he travelled from the team’s base in Charlotte separately from the rest of the team – were attributed to a stomach bug. In fact, it was a heart condition known as atrial fibrillation.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

“You're not going to say I have something to do with my heart two days before the first game of the World Cup,” he said.

“It's not an ideal scenario being in the hospital two days before—well, technically 36 hours before the first game of the World Cup. But you have to take the cards that you're dealt on the chin. It's part of the game. There's nothing I could do about it.”

Some will question the decision to let him play in not only the match against Haiti, which Scotland won 1-0, but also the two following group games against Morocco and Brazil. The Scots lost both fixtures and exited the World Cup with McTominay perceived to have been under par.

“It was in my hands,” he said. “The medical team reassured me it was safe to play and they said: ‘What do you think?' I said: ‘Let’s go for it’.”

Unbeknown to nearly everyone, and while Scotland fans were drinking bars dry in Boston, McTominay was at the centre of incredible drama.

Manager Steve Clarke told reporters that the midfielder had been laid low by a stomach bug. The reality of the situation - and the fact it was kept secret for so long - is barely believable given the global attention on the tournament and that McTominay is Scotland's star player.

He himself sought to downplay the situation on Tuesday at Hampden as he revealed the true story for the first time. “We got a police escort to go and get the shock then that was it to be honest,” recalled McTominay. “After that, I was back in normal rhythm, which is how a healthy heart should be then I went and played the game two days later.”

He described being put under anaesthetic. “You have to get put to sleep,” he said. “Whenever you go under anaesthetic and you have to get put to sleep, it decreases the athletic performance a little bit and (affects) sleep and stuff like that. It was far from ideal but those are the cards that you're dealt, there's nothing you can do about it.”

Although he stressed his family were fully on board with him playing, he wouldn’t have listened had it been otherwise. “All my family and friends had just flown 10 hours for the first game of the World Cup,” he said.

“I didn’t sit there thinking I might not play. That would never be the case. I was always going to play in that game. Maybe selfishly, I don’t know but that’s football. Players play with injuries all the time when they’re not quite right and it might be to the detriment of the team. (But) I was fully functional.”

The Napoli midfielder has since undergone an operation after the problem resurfaced following an early season Serie A game against Como. He returned to Manchester, where he had a procedure known as pulsed field ablation.

The player was sidelined for several weeks, missing the first games under new Scotland manager Sebastien Pocognoli but has returned to the squad for upcoming Nations League games against North Macedonia and Switzerland.

#1955. Scott McTominay: I didn't know what people were saying about me and the World Cup

Picture the scene. Scotland fans are drinking Boston’s bars dry. Meanwhile, unbeknown to them, their star player, their main hope, was getting a police escort to a hospital in the city to have his heartbeat jolted back into a normal pattern. Scotland tend to make a drama out of World Cups, but this is something else.

It is almost a year to the day since Scott McTominay wowed the world with an overhead kick to set Scotland on the way to qualifying for the tournament for the first time in 28 years against Denmark. This might have been expected to be a main topic of conversation as the player sat down for an all-too rare interview at Hampden on Tuesday.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

In the end, however, this scintillating piece of skill, immortalised on a tenement gable end near Hampden, proved barely an afterthought. McTominay consents to interviews only very infrequently, certainly in Scotland. When he does do them, they seem like events.

This is especially the case when he is recalling being blue lighted through the streets of Boston a couple of evenings before Scotland were due to make their long-awaited return to the World Cup against Haiti.

It is scarcely believable that having had his heart effectively reset, he was lining up against the Caribbean nation in a pulsating World Cup encounter a mere 36 hours later. He very nearly even scored.

The Napoli midfielder watched a shot crash off the post in the first half shortly before John McGinn scored with a deflected effort that proved the winner. Although he was so close to getting on the scoresheet, the general perception was that McTominay struggled to shake off the effects of the “stomach bug” that had been communicated as the reason for his absence from training two days beforehand.

The midfielder was considered never to have reached the heights expected of him during Scotland’s tournament, which lasted another two games. It must have been excruciatingly irritating for him to read such verdicts and be unable to respond.

He was even rated in some quarters as among the tournament’s biggest flops. The Scotland staff couldn’t say anything, nor could he. He claims he was oblivious to the criticism.

“I didn’t know that’s what people were saying,” he said. “Although I probably had an idea. I’ve been criticised a million times before in my career before but I don’t let it get under my skin or worry too much about it.

“You know yourself as a professional footballer if you’re not quite where you should be. For me, I had half an idea but you just try to block it out because if you think about negative things you might speak it into existence.”

There might be a lot of people eating humble pie having been informed of the true nature of McTominay’s health problem. It’s no one’s fault. You can’t refer to such a serious mitigating factor if it’s being – understandably – kept hidden. McTominay explained to rapt reporters the details behind his condition, which is known as atrial fibrillation. In other words, an unsteady heartbeat. He even provided some sound effects. Who says McTominay is an unwilling interviewee?

“Atrial fibrillation is a fairly normal routine thing for people in general,” he said. “They might not know that they have it. But when you're an elite athlete in general across the board, across football, across sports in general, you know if you've got something that's different.

“Whenever you're running and you check your pulse and it's got a slight irregular beat there, it feels like your heart's coming out of your chest.

“Not obviously as bad as that but that's the sensation that you have. It's pumping, but not a regular heartbeat like bum, bum, bum, bum. Mine's going bum, bu-bu-bum, bum, bu-bu-bum. So you know the difference.”

You also know that it’s not something you would wish to develop on the eve of the World Cup that is being played in intense temperatures.

“The heat was tough, that was probably the hardest part,” he reflected. “But I’ve worked for 20 years as a young footballer and as a professional to get to that point, to try and play well at a World Cup.” Nothing, he stressed, was going to stop him, not even lying on a hospital bed under anaesthetic two evenings before the first game while an electrode is placed on his chest.

He has since been back in hospital for a more involved procedure. Napoli released a statement in September to say the minimally invasive operation known as cardiac ablation surgery had been “a complete success” although McTominay missed several matches, including the first four Nations League fixtures under new manager Sebastien Pocognoli.

“I went into that surgery with no doubt in my mind that I’d be back,” he said. “I lost a little bit of muscle when I came out, three or four kilos which wasn’t ideal. I had to put that back on pretty sharpish.

“The first picture of me when I came back, I looked quite gaunt. So I had to get that muscle back so I could get back my powerful running and what I normally do on a football pitch.

“It was a good reset period for me,” he added. “No matter how long it took - even if it took until I was 40! - I was coming back to try and do my best. I’ve had a good time to reflect on the World Cup and think about things leading up to it.

“When I had the operation I had three weeks at home. I didn’t watch as much football as I normally do. I (normally) watch every game of football, every night. It’s relentless with me.

“Games in the Champions League, Europa League, Scottish football, the Premier League, Serie A - I watch a lot now compared to when I was younger.

“So I had three weeks of resting my mind more than anything to try and come back in a better state.”

It’s good news for the Tartan Army, who are desperate for McTominay, who turns 30 next month, to rescue Scotland from an unsure start to the Nations League under Pocognoli. The Belgian has stressed he wants to find a way of taking the burden off those such as McTominay. But the player himself doesn’t mind the extra responsibility. Indeed, he relishes it.

“He's mentioned that to me before about maybe taking a little bit (of the burden) and putting it across the whole board, but I don’t see football like that,” he said.

“I don’t go into a game thinking that the people watching really need me to do something here so I try to do different things, you just play the game, don’t you?

“Express yourself and play how you would normally play, and the rest will take care of itself, you don’t need to overthink about pressure.

“I’ve played at Man United, I’ve played at Napoli, I know what pressure is. I’ve played for Scotland in the World Cup, I know what pressure is. It’s not the worst thing in the world that can happen to you. It’s a privilege to have things expected of you.”

Pocognoli told reporters last week that he was looking forward to making a connection with someone generally identified as Scotland’s star player. It seems he is already well on the way to achieving this despite the pair only having met in the flesh for the first time earlier this week.

It was Pocognoli's idea for McTominay to sit down with the media at Hampden on Tuesday, an instruction he obeyed.

“I like his ideas a lot,” said McTominay “Whenever I first had a meeting with him, I liked the way that he wants to play the game.”

At the end of the near 15-minute conversation with McTominay, an annual at best occurrence, there was just about enough time to reference the approaching one-year anniversary of That goal. And mention That 36ft tall mural, which was unveiled earlier this year.

“Unreal,” he said. “I don’t know how I feel. I obviously like it, it’s incredible, but if you were asking me, you don’t want my big ugly face up there!”

However, Pocognoli expressed confidence that manager Marco Rose would utilise the winger more freely given the club’s European commitments.

Gannon-Doak has since featured seven times for Bournemouth, including four starts. He was even named man-of-the-match in the recent 3-0 Europa League win over AC Milan that shocked so many people across Europe. Many had doubted whether he could contribute sustained performances for Scotland while featuring so rarely for Bournemouth.

But Pocognoli, who is hoping to secure his first Hampden victory on Friday night against North Macedonia, is comforted that his forecast that Gannon-Doak would return to England and “smash it” has proved accurate.

If he can improve on being more clinical in front of goal he would probably have scored two goals in the last window.”

Pocognoli has noticed the player is happier taking on responsibility and is displaying more composure. He is thinking more about what to do next when he has the ball rather than absent mindedly throwing it into the box.

“His assist and crossing was more with the idea before ‘if I put a cross in Scott McTominay will make a bicycle kick!’” he said. “But you see a little bit more of him now thinking what the next action is when he’s dribbling. Although it was a slightly underwhelming first international window for Pocognoli, the Belgian believes players such as Gannon-Doak reaped the benefits from the four games.

Scotland won once against North Macedonia, lost 3-0 to Switzerland and drew and lost against Slovenia.

“I said to the lads when they arrived in September there were a lot of players with a lack of minutes,” he recalled.

#1952. Midweek magic follows weekend woe as Eastbourne Borough down Dulwich Hamlet

For Borough supporters, loyalty comes with a sou'wester and a set of waterproofs: only a week ago, after the gale-blown victory over Stanway Rovers, manager Steve King had described the conditions as "horrendous" – and this week's weather was another challenge.

The game began in drizzle and ended in sweeping rain - the sort that, in shimmering floodlights, can look almost picturesque. Almost...

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

But who notices a few drips down your neck when your team is winning? Borough supporters had returned deflated from Dartford, but by the second half of Tuesday's game they were pumped up and roaring again.

Postponed from an October Saturday because of Borough's FA Cup run, the visit of Dulwich Hamlet was just a little anti-climactic. The South London club and their buoyant supporters usually travel in numbers and liven up any game - but the logistics of a Tuesday night journey to the coast are trickier.

Hamlet's own league form has been patchy this season, but they always play without fear and they enjoy nothing better than a game which starts at high pace and then gets quicker.

That was precisely how Tuesday night's action began at the Lane. After two early chances for the Sports from corner-kicks, Hamlet snatched a surprise lead in the sixth minute, with a flicked finish by David Smith just beyond the reach of home keeper Lewis Carey.

The Sports were stirred rather than shaken - and a bit indignant. Chances came and went, but Dulwich were defending deep, and the home side were caught between playing their instinctive purist football or piling forward and getting the ball any which way into the Hamlet penalty area.

Indeed, the visitors were growing in confidence, and they created chances to extend the lead: one smart Lewis Carey save and two excellent interventions, by Max Sheaf and Freddie Carter, snuffed out the openings.

A huge home shout for a penalty was waved away by the referee - but the Sports were not relying on marginal decisions as they suddenly breached the Hamlet defences.

With 25 minutes played, a deep Josh Rees cross was met at the back post by Liam Nash - in his first full game back after injury - and Darren McQueen pounced to slide in the equaliser.

Most games have a turning point and that McQueen finish turned the mood for players, manager and huddled fans - from soaking wet gloom to a sudden sense of relief and optimism.

This Steve King squad is not perfect, but it has spirit, character, experience. And a drenching night at the Lane is no barrier. Within the next ten minutes, Borough had turned the match irreversibly in their favour with a 3-1 lead.

First, Rees pounded through from midfield, took a touch to get his angle right, and drilled past the visiting keeper for 2-1. The momentum had swung, and the belief was back.

And then it was Rees again - team skipper in every sense, and a man who embodies the spirit of drive and enterprise which his manager is demanding - who extended the lead to 3-1. Carter won the ball from Bangura following a Dulwich corner, and he drove forward with posse of four Borough players, before finding McQueen on the right.

The winger cut across to Rees, whose first effort was blocked before he tucked he ball past Sands at the second bite.

Hamlet really did not know what had hit them. From that bright start, they had seen the match ripped away from them.

The second half brought more of the same. In such buffeting conditions against unpredictable opponents, 3-1 was not necessarily a winning score. Hamlet were looking to sit deep and hit Borough on the counter - and they did exactly that with a swift end-to-end break for 3-2.

Anything Hamlet could do, Borough could do better. Liam Nash - in his first full game since a cheekbone injury - was the man on the mark. Kai Corbett brought down Sam Oguntayo's channel pass with ease, and he drove up the wing before crossing low. Paul McCallum dummied for Nash to steal his fifth goal of the season.

The last 20 minutes saw no further drama. Hamlet brought on the ageless Danny Mills, but even his scoring talents could not retrieve this game for the visitors.

#1950. Bradford City midfielder George Lapslie on perspective, family and silver lining with Michael Duff

In the difficult moments, there's a fair degree of empathy. Like earlier this year.

The Bradford City midfielder found himself out of the first-team squad during the 2025-26 run-in and his elder brother was also struggling for opportunities at National League South side Chelmsford City.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

While Lapslie junior had his own issues, he had perspective because his sibling has struggled significantly with injuries throughout his career.

Lapslie told The Yorkshire Post: "I'm in contact with my brother daily. He's now at Farnborough.

"My brother has struggled a lot in his career (with injuries) and it's probably a lot of the reason why I'm so grateful because he's struggled with multiple injuries.

"So if you compare it to what I've had, I've been able to play but I just can't play (not selected) on a matchday compared to not being able to play at all.

"I'm grateful for being able to stay fit and try and help the team when I do get a chance.

"When we speak, we try to keep it unrelated to football. But it came to a point where in March, it was like eight or nine squads in a row where you're not in. Then we're talking about what the future looked like.

"But apart from that, we try and keep it away from football because obviously we're both consumed with football all the time anyway."

The Bantams player has fought his way back into the first-team picture at City and is also hugely grateful for what he's got at a club which is in the Londoner's soul and his family's.

Family is everything to Lapslie and so are City.

His parents are regular visitors to Valley Parade, making the trip up from the south. His nan was also in attendance at the club's EFL Cup win at Leyton Orient earlier this autumn.

There were touching scenes after the game when Lapslie embraced her. His grandfather, who had been a big source of inspiration in his life and a huge supporter, had passed away a few weeks earlier.

The Waltham Forest born player's pride at stepping out in the claret and amber is not the sort that can be manufactured.

When told back in January that his opportunities could be restricted, he backed himself to earn another chance.

Late in the summer window, despite some interest from elsewhere, the 29-year-old did not push for a move.

Although he was brought up at the other end of the country, Bradford feels like home.

He continued: "My eldest is a Bradford fan. I was doing reading with her the other day and the man's name in the book was Brad and she was like: 'oh, Bradford, Bradford!'

"So everything is Bradford at the house. We've got Bradford flags, Bradford stickers. They've (kids) got their Bradford kits, obviously.

"I'm going to follow Bradford for the rest of my life. That's a fact and I'll be very surprised if my eldest doesn't as well.

"My parents probably come up twice a month to come see us. So we get together quite a bit."

Despite spending time on the periphery, Lapslie's relationship with Alexander remained a good one. But it was not lost upon him that a change of manager could work in his favour.

"I think I've done okay and I think more opportunities will come. So, yes, I'm excited and still believe that I can make it really work here."

While Lapslie was left out of Duff's first match-day league squad for the home game against Stevenage on October 17, there was a silver lining.

Lapslie continued: "It speaks volumes about him as well, to take the time to get to know my daughters because he could have easily just moved on there and he didn't. He took the time to get to know us. So yes, I'm really grateful for that."

Josh Rees should actually have scored with the first Borough chance of note. McCallum managed to spray a pass into open space, where Darren McQueen raced to get in on goal. Smith turned provider, flicking the ball to Fiddes, who cut onto his left foot before producing a reversed finish into the far corner.

Dartford made it three through player-manager Greenhalgh just after the half hour. Matthew Hayden made a mess of a clearance and it landed at Greenhalgh’s feet on the edge of the box, and he took a touch to set up a low drive past Carey.

Sandford was determined to keep a clean sheet against his former side as he made another fine stop to deny Rees. Max Sheaf’s cross from deep was pinpoint and met the head of an onrushing Rees. From just six yards, Rees thought he had pulled one back, but Sandford reacted sharply to parry out and behind.

It was the same old story just before half-time as another mistake allowed Fiddes to make it four. A poor pass led to a one-on-one opportunity with Fiddes against Hayden, and Dartford’s forward outmuscled Borough’s number two, before firing into the bottom corner.

The Sports looked for a response in the second 45 as they dominated possession against a stubborn Dartford block. They had to be patient for chances, but just felt it was not their day as they hit the woodwork again. Corbett’s free-kick panicked Sandford but smashed against the bar.

There was a consolation for Borough, and a fitting goal on his return for Nash. Fellow substitute Terrell Egbri’s cross was helped on by Shay Harrison towards Nash, and after miscuing a first attempt, he produced an instinctive scorpion kick into the roof of the net.

#1941. ‘Without doubt’ – Lack of physicality major reason behind Crawley Town’s league position, says interim boss

Having been at the club for three weeks, Blackwell has had ample opportunity to assess the Reds squad.

And the former Leeds and Sheffield United once again highlighted Crawley’s deficiencies.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

He said: “We are neither technical or physical. We are not a totally technical side or a totally physical side.

“We brought Ben [Heneghan] in who is a 6ft 3 centre half, we brought Connor [Wickham] at 6ft 2 up front – we need some more physicality.

“In central midfield we have nobody above 5ft 8. You look at the games against Tranmere and against Oldham, they were physically towering above us yet we’ve shown we have the capabilities to fight.

“It’s not all about just having big boys, it’s about having the desire and the fight to make sure that you win your battle.”

Blackwell also reiterated his concerns surrounding the club’s recruitment.

He added: “Once again, I question the recruitment. If you have six people in midfield and the tallest is 5ft 10 and three are 5ft 8, how do you deal with a 6ft, 6ft 2 midfield player?

“We’ve got to look at balancing the physical and technical side. I see us at the moment being half of one and half of the other and it’s not working.”

League Two is an extremely physical division – and Blackwell admitted the Reds were being ‘bullied’ by opposition teams.

He said: “Without doubt we are getting bullied on the ball. Everybody knows what League Two football is

“We’ve got to look at areas of the pitch we need to be strong – and that’s ironically in both boxes, and then the flare in the wide areas”

“At the moment we haven’t got that so we are trying to address that and that’s what the owners are trying to do.

“We need to try and get through to Christmas and then see if we can maybe change the dynamics of the squad – but knowing full well what is required in this league.”

Following Blackwell’s thorough assessment of the squad, he was rest assured that the board will take on his advice and make the changes required to steer the club away from trouble.

He said: “I think they are well aware themselves of the situation. You’ve only got to watch the games to know that physically we’ve struggled against teams that are more physical than us.

“You bake a cake and the recipe has got to be right. It’s not all about height, it’s also about technical ability, speed, power.

“But every sport is power and pace. We haven’t got enough of that at this moment in time, but we’ve recognised that and are trying to correct it.”

Crawley have signed four free agent in the past fortnight. Now with a squad of 32, Blackwell has the challenge of sorting through the squad and picking his best 11.

He said: “First of all you look at attitude and you look at ability and you look at what they do in training everyday. Tthat’s a big for any coach what they do on the training ground, and that can influence your decision.

“I’ve seen these now for two weeks. I’ve seen them on the training ground, I’ve now seen them in the game and all my experience in the game tells me I know what they can do and what they can’t do.”

The Reds now have an extended break before their next game, having had this weekend’s game against Rotherham postponed.

When asked how he would tackle this next week, Blackwell said: “The great thing about football is everyday is different and problems arise out of nowhere sometimes, but the good thing for the next few weeks is that we’ve got no game in hand.

“We can now concentrate on the training ground. We are focussing on Fleetwood and how we are going to try and get a result against Fleetwood.”

His co-host Hutton added to Stewart’s complaints, saying: “It's not a penalty. He barely touches him. Like I said, all contact in the box isn't a penalty kick. Am I right in saying the referee gave it on the pitch? I think it should be overturned [by VAR]. If anybody showed me this on VAR, I would know first time that wasn't a foul. It needed to be overturned.”

Despite the duo’s frustration at the Rangers penalty being awarded, former English Premier League referee Dermot Gallagher backed Walsh on Sky Sports' Ref Watch programme, claiming “no one” had a better view than the referee and that he made the correct on field decision.

“The defender definitely doesn't get the ball,” said Gallagher. “Look where the referee is, he's got the perfect view. There's the ball, Rangers player plays the ball, he doesn't, it's very hard to go against the referee in that situation.” Fellow Sky Sports guest, and former Aston Villa manager, Tim Sherwood agreed with him, saying: “It’s a minimal touch, but we're happy [that it’s a penalty].”

#1937. Charlie wins battle of the Savages! Son scores in 5-0 FA Cup hammering of dad Robbie's Peterborough United - as manager appears to try and supress smile

Published: 17:03 EST, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 17:26 EST, 7 November 2026

Charlie Savage came out on top in the FA Cup's Battle of the Savages with a goal against his dad Robbie's new team, Peterborough United.

Already two goals up thanks to strikes by Daniel Kyerewaa and Jack Marriott, Reading made a place in round two virtually secure when Robbie's son Charlie added a third in first-half stoppage time.

The midfielder, 23, latched on to a loose ball on the edge of the Peterborough area and fired home, with the aid of a slight deflection, before racing off towards the visiting fans and celebrating with a knee slide.

Dad Robbie, who took over as Posh boss last month after his stint at Forest Green Rovers, looked initially frustrated at his team's defending but you almost sensed a smile given the identity of the goalscorer.

'Charlie Savage's goal is all about him seeing the danger, holding his run, letting it run across his body and finishing,' said former Reading midfielder Steve Sidwell on BBC Sport. 'Reading are deservedly in charge of the game, and Savage has been superb.'

Former Leicester midfielder and Wales international Robbie had feared as much in an exclusive interview with the Daily Mail before the first-round tie.

Charlie Savage scores against his dad Robbie’s side! 😳Reading make it 3-0 at Peterborough! 🔥📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/RmMzxfNIzE

'Charlie Savege's goal is all about him seeing the danger, holding his run, letting it run across his body and finishing,' said former Reading midfielder Steve Sidwell

Savage Jnr celebrates with a knee slide that his dad would have been proud of

Charlie takes advice from the Reading bench as his father Robbie (centre) looks on

'It's going to be horrible,' he had said. 'Every time I watch my sons play, I'm anxious. I'm nervous. I want them to do well. If they give the ball away and the other team attack, I've got butterflies thinking, "Please don't score".

That particular wish took on a new meaning as his lad lined up to shoot with his left foot to strengthen Reading's vice-like grip on the tie.

Like his dad, Charlie came through Manchester United's youth ranks and made one first-team appearance, as a substitute at the age of 18 against Young Boys in the Champions League. It was an unforgettable night for Robbie, who was on co-commentary duty with a lump in his throat.

Much the same applied on Saturday night, though this time there were mixed emotions in the Savage household.

It got worse, much worse, as Jamie Reid netted twice in the second half to make it 5-0 to the visitors.

Peterborough can now focus on improving their position from third bottom of League One, while Reading may wish to put thoughts of Wembley to one side as they set their sights on a promotion push.

#1935. Michael Carrick responds to Man Utd relegation fears after Aston Villa draw

Michael Carrick downplayed fears Manchester United were in a relegation battle after a remarkable 4-4 draw with Aston Villa in the Premier League.

United will sit in the relegation zone of the Premier League during the November international break after a thrilling 4-4 draw with Villa at Old Trafford.

Aston Villa twice led by two goals but Manchester United produced two spirited fightbacks to avoid defeat and potentially prolong Carrick’s reign as manager.

Goals from Brazilian winger Alysson and Senegal striker Nicolas Jackson put Villa 2-0 up inside five minutes but the hosts were level by half-time thanks to Bruno Fernandes’ penalty and Youri Tielemans equaliser against his former club.

John McGinn restored Aston Villa’s lead just after half-time and the visitors appeared to have the game wrapped up when Leon Goretzka scored a fourth on 53 minutes.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

But injury-time goals from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu saw Manchester United salvage a point and avoid a third successive league defeat.

The comeback rivalled the one United produced in the Champions League against Roma during the week but it remains to be seen whether it saves Carrick his job.

Despite avoiding defeat, the Red Devils slip to 18th in the Premier League after ten games, their lowest position at the stage of a campaign since 1986.

Carrick’s side have also gone eight league games without a win, matching a run they have endured just once before in the Premier League.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘I’m disappointed that we haven’t won the game,’ Carrick said. ‘We looked the better team for long parts of it and we’re making it difficult for ourselves with the goals that we’re giving away.

‘We’re not just giving away one, it’s two in succession that put us in such a difficult position. We did it the other night, we did it again today and have come back into the game and had a lot of the game, could have won it at the end.

‘So I’m disappointed we haven’t won the game. It’s just moments that we need to tighten up on. Individual moments where we’re giving teams goals that we don’t normally get.

‘If we tighten up that, there’s a lot of good in that performance. I thought we should have won the game. But conceding the goals we are is not helping us at all.

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 pic.twitter.com/q1fBKSXL7l

‘We have got to tighten up, it’s pretty obvious to say that. It’s giving us too much to do in games. But I thought we did a lot and feel that we should have won the game.’

Asked whether he feels Manchester United are in a relegation battle, Carrick added: ‘We’re in November. I don’t like this situation or the results but we can definitely do something about it.’

Responding to Carrick’s post-match interview, former Manchester United captain Roy Keane said: ‘It’s obviously difficult for the manager. He’s under pressure, no doubt

‘He talks a lot but doesn’t say much. I don’t know if that’s a tactic. Like a politician. He keeps saying we need to tighten up and there’s things we need to work on.

‘But they better get moving on that. It’s the worst start in how many years, all these stats aren’t very good. If you keep giving up goals and chances, it’s just going to continue.

‘What are we expecting to change over the next few weeks and months? What are they working on? They need to do a lot better than that.’

While Manchester United slipped into the relegation zone, Aston Villa stay 10th after extending their unbeaten league run to seven games.

#1934. Bradford City 4 York City 0: Clean EFL Trophy sweep for Bantams who show ruthless side again

BD8 was packed to the rafters just 10 days earlier for Bradford City’s juicy league meeting with Huddersfield Town.

On this occasion, in front of an understandably sparse crowd, the atmosphere was low octane in comparison.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

For those that ventured out, including a decent-sized following of almost 700 supporters from the walled city - with York making their first visit to this part of West Yorkshire since October 2012 - it proved worth their while, even if there was little riding on this final Northern Group C game.

Bradford were through, most likely as group winners unless something silly happened. Which it definitely didn’t.

A first-half opener from returning captain Antoni Sarcevic - whose three goals this term have all been on home soil - put the hosts on their way to a clean sweep of group victories.

A third cup strike of the campaign for Stephen Humphrys rubber-stamped the win before another striker with a penchant for goals in knock-out football this season in Will Swan provided gloss.

Swan’s 70th-minute strike, nine minutes after Humphrys’ goal, took his season’s goal tally to seven, with just one in the league.

Substitute Nick Powell joined in the goalscoring action before the end after his midweek brace in the cup against Marine. He is now one shy of double figures.

It was a rewarding night for Michael Duff’s side, whose next two fixtures arrive against White Rose visitors in the shape of Doncaster Rovers and Barnsley. This was a decent warm-up.

With the pressure maybe off a touch, both sets of players among much-changed line-ups, showed good things for the first hour, more especially those in claret and amber.

York’s wait for a first away win on their league return goes on, as does their run without a victory in Bradford - the Minstermen last won here in March 1980.

For 60 minutes, they gave a good account of themselves before the Bantams showed the ruthless edge which mauled Marine. The scoreline was cruel on them on the night.

City made ten changes from their handsome cup slaying of Marine, with Kieran Morgan being the only player who lined up against the Merseysiders.

It was a notable night for Iraq under-23 goalkeeper Zac Hadi, handed a Bantams debut, while Harry Ibbitson started for the first time at Valley Parade.

Fresh from his one-match suspension, Sarcevic got a run-out for the hosts, inactive after this fixture until November 21.

Unlike the Bantams, York were mindful of forthcoming weekend league business at Rochdale. Scott Lindsey not only changed his entire XI from the weekend cup victory over Northampton Town, but gave them the complete night off with none on the bench either.

The Minstermen gave a debut to youngster Lewis Beadle, with keeper George Sykes-Kenworthy getting the nod in goal at the club where he started out.

Bradford led at the break, but both sides contributed to a very watchable contest, more especially given that it was a ‘dead rubber’.

The Bantams and their visitors both hit the woodwork. York played some neat passing football at times, but it was the hosts who drew first blood with an elegant 32nd-minute opener.

The hosts broke with intent and Swan’s perceptive left-wing cross found Humphreys, who spotted Sarcevic in space and found him with a lovely weighted pass and the home captain finished clinically, low past Sykes-Kenworthy - as befitting a goalscoring midfielder of his ilk. It was a quality move and finish.

Humphreys and Sarcevic had some fun in the final period of the half and had further chances, with York starting to look a bit wary. They had brought offerings to the table before that at the other end.

Hadi was forced into significant work to make a strong double save to deny Jovan Malcolm and Joe Grey before producing a textbook parry - and positioning - to keep out Dipo Akinyemi’s goalbound header.

Earlier, York knocked on wood from close range, courtesy of Ethan Shiver. As did Bradford earlier, with Kieran Morgan displaying sublime technique to warm up a nippy November night. His exquisite shot with the outside of his foot clipped the post.

Half-time came at a more convenient juncture for York than the hosts. But it was Bradford who carried on from where they left off ahead of the interval, with Morgan - having a handy game - finding Swan, whose rasping shot stung the palms of Sykes-Kenworthy.

The York custodian was then called into action again to beat out Humphrys’ angled drive, with Sarcevic’s follow-up header hitting the underside of the bar.

In keeping with an entertaining evening, York should have levelled moments later.

Malcolm broke away and went for glory instead of slotting in Akinyemi. Hadi, in keeping with his good night, made himself big and made the point-blank save.

It’s importance was soon magnified when Humphreys’ header doubled the hosts lead just after the hour mark following Reece Welsh’s right-wing centre.

It was Humphrys' last involvement of the night.

Swan tucked home a third following substitute Powell’s cross after the Minstermen were opened up.

City gave debuts off the bench in the final quarter to two youngsters in Leeroy Gomes, Gabe Holt and Oliver Hewitt.

Powell added an effortless late fourth after clever play by the impressive Morgan. A rewarding night for Bradford.

Bradford City: Hadi; Welch, Matthews, Pratt (Hewitt 85); Ibbitson, Cartwright, Morgan, O'Keeffe (Holt 77); Sarcevic (Lunn 62), Swan (Gomes 77); Humphrys (Powell 62). Substitutes unused: Doyle, Gillesphey.

York City: Sykes-Kenworthy; J Hunt, Beadle, Medley (Belleh 62); King, Maguire, Stiver, Grey (Farrar 62), Newby; Malcolm, Akinyemi. Substitutes unused: White, Swansbury, Ozisik, Penrose, Appleyard.

#1933. Roy Keane criticises Senne Lammens after Manchester United draw with Aston Villa

Roy Keane said the form of goalkeeper Senne Lammens is ‘hurting’ Manchester United after a thrilling 4-4 draw with Aston Villa.

Lammens endured another difficult game as Michael Carrick’s side conceded four goals at home to Villa.

The Belgian shot-stopper was nutmegged by Alysson inside two minutes and then could only parry a shot into the path of Nicolas Jackson who doubled Villa’s lead on four minutes.

The writing appeared to be on the wall for under-fire manager Carrick but United responded and were level at half-time thanks to Bruno Fernandes’ penalty and Youri Tielemans’ strike against his former club.

Aston Villa once again opened up a two-goal lead early into the second half, John McGinn scoring a penalty before Leon Goretzka poked home the visitors’ fourth.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

But Manchester United scored two injury-time goals through substitutes Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu to avoid defeat and salvage an unlikely point.

Despite two spirited fightbacks, an eighth league game without a win leaves the Red Devils in the relegation zone heading into the November international break.

Former Manchester United captain Keane was left with wildly mixed emotions after the game, criticising the poor defensive display but praising the team for showing ‘a bit of fight and desire’.

‘There have been question marks over this team showing a bit of fight, a bit of desire,’ Keane told Sky Sports. ‘And as bad as the game was from a football point of view they kept going until the end.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘They kept going, so you have to give them a little bit of praise. But in terms of the bigger picture it’s that rollercoaster of watching United.

‘Some bits were so, so bad. Defensively, the start to the first half, the start to the second half, but they found a way to get a point when they looked dead and buried.

‘Ultimately nowhere near good enough to try to get towards the middle of the table. They can do a lot better than what they’re doing. We saw evidence of that last year, when they went on the run they went in.

‘They’ve lost Casemiro, an important, experienced player for them. They certainly should be doing a lot better.

"You've got to be hard to beat" ❌Roy Keane talks about Manchester United lacking the "basics" pic.twitter.com/TnkdbchtcG

‘We go back to some of the basics. The way they’re starting games, the way they’re coming out for the second half. There are things they can improve on.

‘They’re probably lacking a bit of confidence but if you’re giving up four goals at home, you make it so hard for yourself.

‘When they were on a good run of results last year, the goalkeeper was doing very well, making a lot of big saves, he’s not doing that. Bruno was on fire, he’s not at his very best at the moment.

‘The goalkeeper has to do better. It doesn’t help if your goalkeeper isn’t making saves, that hurts the team a lot.

‘So there are some basic footballing reasons… but to be in the bottom three, playing for Man Utd… this should be hurting them.’

#1932. Gary Neville names four players who will ‘get Man Utd relegated’ after Aston Villa draw

Gary Neville has slammed Manchester United’s failure to sign any new defenders last summer and says the back-four that finished the remarkable 4-4 draw with Aston Villa will ‘get the club relegated’.

The Premier League giants go into the November international break sitting 18th in the table after Villa twice blew two-goal leads to draw at Old Trafford.

United found themselves 2-0 down inside five minutes as Alysson and Nicolas Jackson took advantage of the hosts’ fragile defence.

Michael Carrick’s side were level at half-time thanks to Bruno Fernandes’ penalty and Youri Tielemans’ 44th-minute strike against the club he left last summer

Josh McGinn restored Aston Villa’s lead with a penalty straight after the interval and the visitors looked on course for a big win when Leon Goretzka scored a fourth.

Read exclusive analysis of the biggest stories in football with Metro's weekly football newsletter In The Mixer. Sign up now for free.

But Manchester United scored twice in injury-time – substitutes Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu with the goals – to salvage a point and avoid sitting joint-bottom during the international break.

Despite two comebacks, United’s current position is their lowest at this stage of a season since 1986, while their eight-game winless league run has only happened once before.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Manchester United finished the Aston Villa thriller with a back-four of Noussair Mazraoui, Leny Yoro, Ayden Heaven and Patrick Dorgu, and Neville said that line-up would struggle to avoid relegation to the Championship.

‘The reason Manchester United have conceded four goals is because they haven’t invested in the defence in the transfer window,’ he said on NBC Sports.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘Every one knew they had to do that, they needed defenders. The current ones are making mistake after mistake after mistake.

‘The defenders that finished that game will get you relegated. Watch the defensive errors… we all screamed in the transfer window that they have to bring some defenders in.

‘They had to bring the transfer budget forward and bring defenders in.’

Gary’s brother Phil, who also enjoyed incredible success at Manchester United as a player, added: ‘The back-four that finished the game – Mazraoui, Yoro, Heaven and Dorgu – that gets you relegated.

"Should be banging heads!" 😡Roy Keane discusses how Manchester United can improve their form pic.twitter.com/r7JZzj62LD

‘That back-four gets you the sack as a manager and that back-four cannot keep United, I don’t think, in the Premier League.

‘That back-four gets you relegated, it’s poor. It’s not good enough to play in the Premier League.’

Despite Manchester United’s grim position in the Premier League, Gary Neville doubts a change in the dugout would improve the situation in the long-term.

‘You can paper over the cracks and get a new manager bounce,’ he added. ‘When the new manager comes in, everybody’s happy for a couple of months and all of a sudden, six months later, it happens again.

‘You can keep changing the manager and thinking that’s going to be the answer. But this has been proven now over eight managers in 12 years, that’s not the answer.

‘Michael could leave, Michael might stay, we don’t know, the ownership don’t have a clue what to do.

‘It’s rinse and repeat. Amorim, Ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Carrick, Jose Mourinho, Louis van Gaal, David Moyes, Ralf Rangnick – some of them are world class managers who have had success, there are a lot of promising young managers there, ex players who know the club as well.

‘None of it has worked because if you recruit badly, if you’ve got poor performance department, poor recruitment department, you’ve not got leadership that is strong right through the spine of the football club you will fail.

‘Every organisation in the world will fail if you’ve not got an aligned leadership from top to bottom – your board and your ownership right the way through to the person who is stood on the pitch trying to play football.

‘There are real issues within that football club, you’ve got people doing those jobs who have never done those jobs before in senior positions.’
